To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the increase in N2O emission from agricultural soils induced by the use and management of Nr in agriculture is compensated by the uptake of CO2 by nonagricultural ecosystems, so that Nr use in agriculture does not contribute to global warming.

the increase in N2O emission from agricultural soils due to the use of Nr is completely compensated by increased carbon storage in nonagriculture soils, but the overall impact of N2O emissions on global warming is positive.

‘Nr inputs to agricultural systems cause an increase of N2O emission that is completely counteracted in the global warming potential by the increase in carbon sequestration due to Nr inputs to terrestrial nonagriculture systems, and that the overall effect of Nr inputs to agricultural systems is therefore neutral for the GWP.’
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (1) What is the global warming potential of nitrogen (Nr)-induced emissions of carbon dioxide (CO₂), nitrous oxide and methane?
the quantification of the global warming potential of nitrogen (Nr)-use in European agriculture.
the development of a method to quantify the global warming potential of nitrogen (Nr), which is used in agriculture and which is emitted to the atmosphere as ammonia (NH3) and nitrous oxide ( N2O).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Nr use in agriculture does not increase the GWP, and therefore, it cannot be considered a greenhouse gas problem.
Nr use in agriculture has a neutral effect on the global warming, but that the use of Nr has a negative effect on biodiversity and human health and a positive effect on eutrophication.
Nr use in agriculture does not contribute to global warming.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
N use in agriculture has a small positive impact on global warming, but this is completely counteracted if N use in agriculture is accompanied by measures that enhance carbon sequestration.
the use of N in agriculture is not a major source of GWP, but it is a major source of eutrophication.
the use of Nr is not a net source of GHG in Europe, but that the net effect is strongly dependent on the type of Nr input.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the impact on GWP of Nr use in European agriculture is small compared with the impact on GGP of CO2 emissions from fossil fuels.
the use of Nr has a net positive effect on the global climate, which needs to be taken into account in the development of mitigation measures.
, at European level, N-induced emissions of N2O and CO2 are counteracting and that the overall GWP of N use in agriculture is neutral.
